RQLM Part Four — Presented Paths, Device-Local Loops, Stream DMA, and the E-Tree Integration Boundary
Don Gunter — WodansEye Research Series — Closing experimental paper

Abstract
The first three experimental parts began with a NAND memory, crossed into a bounded coherent NAND execution loop, and then separated quantum execution history from the six-address micro-instruction pointer and the visible architectural instruction pointer.
Part Four closes the experimental series by identifying the machine boundary that those experiments were approaching.
The device is the circuit.
Each device is represented classically by an object that owns the construction code for its bounded quantum circuit. The object also owns the bridge between classical supervision and quantum execution:
build
present
pull
run
insert tap
profile
measure
reportA device may be as small as a reversible NAND primitive or as complex as a processor-like local loop, a Rauf local-model controller, a memory hierarchy, an imported circuit supplied by another researcher, or a classical service with a quantum-facing port.
The system bus is therefore divided into two selections:
device / port bus → which device is opened
subaddress bus → which path inside that device is openedThe quantum payload is not treated as a classical word copied across a data bus. A quantum DMA device temporarily joins a source path and destination path, holds a stream open for a bounded interaction, drains its temporary routing state, closes the stream, and presents completion.
The accompanying one-file Python lab contains its own exact statevector simulator, device builders, bridge, buses, parent-loop scheduler, thread manager, DMA stream, QSM-style resource catalog, model builder, OpenQASM 3 bridge, Graphviz exporters, main, and sixteen automated tests. The tests establish software and reversible-circuit plausibility. They do not prove a physical coherent bus, fault tolerance, quantum advantage, or an unbounded quantum computer.
Part Four concludes that the RQLM device model is a credible separate research direction and that E-Tree is an appropriate application architecture for integrating such devices without forcing every device to share one internal design.

Claim labels

• [BUILT] — implemented in the companion one-file reference program.

• [TESTED] — exercised by an automated exact-statevector test with stated expectations.

• [DM] — a mapping between software architecture, circuit construction, and quantum execution.

• [DESIGN] — an architectural choice not established as physical hardware.

• [OPEN] — unresolved research or engineering question.

1. Where the experimental series arrived
Part One established a classical memory rule:
Address selects. Data transfers separately.
Part Two established a bounded coherent execution interval:

• reversible NAND A, B, and C;

• NAND C becoming the next recurrent state;

• path-indexed local models;

• an active-history tape that is both loop memory and a unary execution record;

• compute, retain the needed result, and uncompute scratch;

• one final commit boundary rather than measurement after every primitive.
Part Three then exposed an important correction:
execution history ≠ micro-IP ≠ visible architectural IPThe history tape says which bounded circuit positions were reached. The six-address μIP says which processor-control block is active. The visible IP says which program-visible instruction address the processor is on.
Part Four adds a second correction:
system device selection ≠ internal device subaddressThe line previously called the system address bus is more accurately the device bus, destination bus, or port bus. It selects a device-level T.
The real address bus is the subaddress bus inside the selected device.
Device bus:
Memory 0
Core 0
Core 1
Rauf Controller 0
NAND 12
Quantum DMA 0
Network Interface 0Subaddress bus after Memory 0 is selected:
Bank 2 / Path 7 / Mode 1 / Slot 12This correction lets one memory device hold many qubits and deep coherent structures. It also lets one processor device contain a complete local loop rather than pretending that every gate is separately addressed by the root machine.
1.1 The recovered lineage: QSM, DMPL, Rauf, E-Tree, and QASM
This architecture is a consolidation rather than an accidental change of subject.
QSM
resource identity and experiment harnessDMPL / Diamond
model-driven bounded constructionRauf
local adaptive models and local residualsRQLM
device-local coherent execution and stream DMAE-Tree
T operations, resource graph, providers, leases, applicationsOpenQASM 3
portable compiled circuit artifactThe earlier QSM direction became too large when it tried to reproduce too much of a conventional CPU inside the QPU. The Rauf local-machine architecture supplied the missing correction: a CPU loop is one possible device, not the owner of every quantum resource.
OpenQASM now belongs at the bridge boundary. E-Tree models and resource identities compile to QASM artifacts; imported QASM circuits may be wrapped as guest devices. QASM does not replace the semantic device model or the resource graph.

2. The signed T remains the architecture atom
The architecture atom has three faces.
T⁰ ground / persistent architecture
T⁻ pull / request / microcode
T⁺ presentation / code path / continuation2.1 T⁰: architectural ground
T⁰ holds what persists:

• identity;

• parent and child relations;

• ports;

• internal subaddresses;

• local circuit construction;

• allowed couplings;

• local state ownership;

• neutral or isolated condition.
It is not Boolean zero.
2.2 T⁻: pull
T⁻ expresses what a parent, controller, or destination requests:

• select this device;

• select this internal path;

• open this destination;

• construct this operation;

• attach this stream;

• execute this microstep;

• uncompute this temporary history;

• yield at this boundary.
2.3 T⁺: presentation
T⁺ expresses what is available:

• a ready device port;

• an internal path;

• a thread continuation;

• a memory structure;

• a core-ready state;

• a result path;

• a completion condition.
The circuit does not push a measured value into the next circuit. It presents a path. The parent or destination pulls a compatible relation into being.

3. The device is the circuit
A device is not merely a numerical identifier on a bus. It is a bounded construction with an external contract.
QuantumDevice {
identity
device kind
ports
subaddresses
local state paths
circuit builder
local loop
bridge events
profiling metadata
}The central class operation is:
construct(CircuitPlan)The class owns the code that builds its quantum circuit. This is the equivalent of a circuit factory or builder pattern.
Examples:
NandDevice.construct(plan)
emits reversible NAND gatesMemoryDevice.construct(plan)
may emit no gate until a path is requestedRaufLocalModelDevice.construct(plan)
emits one bounded local model and residual relationExternalCircuitDevice.construct(plan)
delegates to another researcher's circuit factoryClassicalServiceDevice.construct(plan)
emits no quantum gates by default
but still participates through a classical bridge and device portThe object is classical. The circuit it constructs is quantum. Keeping that layer boundary explicit prevents software objects from being confused with qubits.

4. The bridge contract
Every device should be reachable through the same bridge surface even when its internal circuit is different.
DeviceBridge {
build
run
measure
profile
report
insert_tap
}4.1 Build
build asks selected device classes to append their circuits into a bounded circuit plan.
The plan contains:

• qubit allocation;

• gates;

• taps;

• labels;

• selected devices;

• profiling metadata.
The first reference implementation supports:
X
H
CX
CCX
SWAPThat is enough to test reversible NAND, path independence, taps, and the first DMA stream semantics.
4.2 Run
run sends the completed plan to a backend.
The included backend is a small exact statevector simulator. A future adapter may send the same device-built plan into:

• Qiskit;

• another circuit framework;

• a hardware-specific compiler;

• a custom simulator;

• a future physical device interface.
The device class should not need to know which backend receives it unless the circuit requires backend-specific features.
4.3 Measure
Measurement is explicit.
A device does not measure simply because another device accesses it. The bridge measures only named endpoints at a requested commit boundary.
4.4 Insert tap
A tap is instrumentation, not automatically a detector.
In the exact simulator, a tap records the probability distribution at a named point without changing the simulated state. In hardware, a non-destructive equivalent would require a valid coherent probe construction; a classical statevector snapshot is not itself a physical operation.
This distinction must remain visible:
simulator tap → inspect simulation state
coherent hardware tap → reversible interaction to be designed
measurement tap → explicit collapse boundary4.5 Profile and report
The bridge records:

• logical qubits;

• gate counts;

• literal depth;

• two-qubit operations;

• three-qubit operations;

• taps;

• devices;

• subaddresses;

• local cycle counts;

• DMA stream events.
Profiling belongs beside construction because two classes implementing the same device contract may have very different circuit cost.

5. Devices can have different internal intelligence
The device interface does not require every device to be processor-like.
5.1 Dumb device
A reversible NAND device has a small fixed construction:
target ^= NAND(left, right)It waits until its operands and target path are presented and pulled.
5.2 Stateful memory device
A memory device may contain:

• many qubits;

• banks;

• model state;

• history;

• ancillas;

• local indexing;

• local error correction in a future implementation;

• multiple modes associated with one physical path.
One selected memory device is not one bit.
one memory device
→ many subaddresses
→ each subaddress may expose a qubit or deeper structure5.3 Processor-like device
A core or controller device may contain its own bounded microcode loop.
It can operate locally while isolated from the shared buses. It presents a bus request only when it requires another device.
5.4 Rauf local-model device
A Rauf device may own:

• local state;

• observation path;

• coefficients or coefficient references;

• prediction circuit;

• residual circuit;

• continuation rule;

• local adaptation bridge.
Several devices may each implement a different local model or controller. The E-Tree parent may organize them by neighborhood, state region, model family, or destination.
5.5 Imported circuit device
A device adapter may wrap another researcher’s circuit:
ExternalCircuitDevice(
factory = supplied circuit builder,
source_note = provenance and assumptions
)The adapter preserves the other circuit’s internal design while giving it the shared bridge contract.
5.6 Classical service device
An LLM, conventional optimizer, sensor service, or network stack can be represented as a classical service device.
It does not become quantum merely because it is connected to the E-Tree.
Its port may:

• prepare a bounded input;

• submit construction parameters;

• receive final measurement;

• update a local model;

• request a device stream;

• provide a classical continuation.
The same device tree can therefore contain quantum circuits and ordinary software services without erasing the layer boundary.

6. Local cycles create parallelism
Parallelism does not require every device to own the shared bus simultaneously.
A device has a simple external lifecycle:

run local loopPRESENTING
expose request or continuationATTACHED
share selected bus pathsYIELDED
detach and resume local loopWhile isolated:
Core 0 runs local thread A.
Core 1 runs local thread B.
Memory bank performs local maintenance.
